name: Zane Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you truly think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy toys, party goods and seasonal decorations for Jollyway Trading, which supplies toy shops and discount chains. Right now, in November, it's Christmas madness, with containers coming in from the ports and me chasing every late one. I use an AI tool every morning to scan what's trending, check supplier prices and draft my emails, and then I'm on calls with the factories. Stuart Keane owns the business and Lena is the senior buyer. I've been here three years, still the junior, and honestly still learning what sells.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Priya runs a home daycare, she looks after six little ones in our front room, and we've got Arjun, twelve, and Meera, eight. We live in Oakfield and have a mortgage, but we've got more than six months saved plus some shares. We go to the temple on Sundays and help out with the community kitchen once a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the market sort it out, I never believed the big promises. At work I'd say we should keep using it where it earns its keep. To friends I'd say a good tool makes a good worker better, it doesn't replace a good worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I already use it to save an hour a day and it makes me look sharper than my three years deserve. If it never gets better, I've still got that edge over buyers who don't try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the tools and take more of the supplier negotiations. I'd put aside 300 a month toward my own small import idea, maybe selling toys through a small online shop later. And I'd keep helping Priya with the daycare numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit pleased with myself. It's a nice position to be in, a steady job, a good cushion and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every morning. What would it mean if it plateaued?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stuart likes saving money, and he's noticed I'm quicker. He doesn't understand how I do it, but he likes the results. I'd say he sees the value of it, though he'd never use it himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think your boss sees the same value in it that you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the market wins. The firms that use it well do better, and those who don't get left behind. I'd rather be the one who's using it.

To friends I'd say it doesn't **replace** a good worker.

Put **300** a month toward my own small import idea.
Keep helping Priya with the **daycare** numbers.
feel: **Calm** and a bit pleased with myself, with a steady job, a good cushion and a plan.
S0.quote: A good tool makes a good worker better, it doesn't replace a good worker.
fieldNote: Confident because he already uses AI and keeps a plan for his own business.
Free-market instinct: let competition sort out who uses tools well.
Priya's daycare is a second **income** and a family safety net.

steps.text: Take on more supplier negotiations with Lena
Put 300 a month toward his own import idea
Learn two more AI buying tools this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for business and bad for people who stand still. At work I'd say let's use it to grow, not just to cut. To friends I'd say we should keep government out of the way, but business should train its own people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say my kind of job shrinks. AI is good at trend scanning, price comparison and supplier emails, which is half my day. A team of four buyers could be two buyers and a tool, and I'm the junior of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the import side business in earnest, maybe sourcing party goods for small shops. I'd take on the AI project at Jollyway before anyone else does, so I'm the one they need. I'd also use the next year's bonus to build a small stock of goods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy together. I like being ahead of the curve, but I know being ahead isn't the same as being safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jollyway look like with fewer buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably two or three buyers and one clever tool, and Stuart choosing the ones who can run the tool. That's why I'm trying to be the one running it. Lena would stay, she has the relationships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about being the junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I've got Priya's income, savings and a bit of nerve, and I'd say my adaptability counts for something. I'd rather face the question now than have it come when I'm fifty.

To friends I'd say government should stay out of the way, but business should **train** its own people.

Combines an inside move with an **outside** side business.
Free-market framing: government out of the way, firms train their own.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the AI buying project at Jollyway
Start sourcing party goods for small shops on the side
Use next year's bonus to buy a first stock of goods

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the end of a lot of desk jobs and we have to be honest about that. At work I'd say we should use the next year to build something new. To friends I'd say do not wait for the government, build your own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within two years my buying job is done. AGI will find, compare and negotiate better than I can. Robots come about three years after, so the dockers and the warehouse, and Priya's daycare, are safe a lot longer than my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Jollyway in the first year, once I had a few clients lined up, and run the import business full time. I'd use some of the savings to buy stock and a good supplier contract, and keep a safe six months in cash for the mortgage. And I'd find a bookkeeper at the temple, so I'm not doing it all myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, no point pretending. I'm excited by building but frightened by the timing, with two kids and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do with Jollyway and with your own plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's safe, because it's hands-on and trusted care, and parents want a person with their toddler. That gives us a steady base while I do the risky bit. Priya's income would be the rock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Priya's daycare, does AI touch it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even in a fast world, the business only works if there's a human in it that people trust. I'd rather start now with a small stock of toys than wait for a dismissal letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to build our own, so let's get going. At work I'd say let's be the company that uses it best. To friends I'd say let business lead and let families look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best of the three for me. I keep the job a couple of years while I grow the import business on the side, and leave before AGI makes the desk obsolete. In five years I could have a real business with a few staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at Jollyway for two years and run the side business in evenings and weekends. Year one I'd put 500 a month into stock and shipping. Then I'd take on one assistant and see if it can carry itself before I walk out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite good, honestly. Uneasy, because it's still a risk, but a good risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Is it better to wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not wait, but not rush either. Five years is enough to test the idea and decide, and the firm's salary pays for the experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn to build something, be it a bench, a company or a website. Learn to sell as well as to make. And listen to your grandparents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and the good ones will use it. At work I'd say keep growing. To friends I'd say, get a skill, save some money, and don't depend on any one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my buying job will change a lot, but I'd be ready. In ten years I'd be fifty-three, the kids nearly grown, and my business might be running well enough that AGI makes it cheaper rather than killing it. I'd be happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, build the business bit by bit, and invest in shares and a rental flat or two. I'd keep learning the AI tools so my business uses them well. And I'd put some money aside for Arjun's and Meera's studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bored, to tell the truth, because I like a challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is this the easy one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take longer to build, with less risk. I'd test two or three products before the big bet. I'd probably start at the temple's community fair, selling stuff for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently now, if you knew it was ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the future belongs to people who can start things and look after things. I'd also say respect your elders, because they teach you what no tool can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be starting a business under pressure, with a mortgage and two kids. What would help is a few more months of runway, lighter red tape for small firms, and the community around us. Priya's daycare is the rock.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm optimistic about people, not about institutions. If you give a man the freedom to try, he'll find a way. I'd just want a decent safety net behind him, built by families and communities rather than a big state.

headlineQuote: If you give a man the freedom to try, he'll find a way.
portrait: Zane is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at Jollyway Trading, buying toys, party goods and seasonal decorations for toy shops and discount chains.
He uses AI **every day**, is free-market and traditional, and wants to start his own import business.
Priya runs a home daycare, they have two children, a mortgage and more than six months of savings plus shares.
He expects his desk job to end in the AGI worlds and plans to **leave** on his own timing.
He blames slow **institutions**, wants lighter rules for small firms, and trusts family and community as the safety net.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because he would start a business under mortgage pressure.
whatWouldHelp: More **runway**, lighter red tape for small firms, and family and community support.
